newsitem.title: USA: Turkey calls for help to offset pipeline losses.
newsitem.headline: Turkey calls for help to offset pipeline losses.

text.p: Turkey should be compensated for the $27 billion it says it has lost since closing a pipeline that carried Iraqi oil across its territory, Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said on Thursday.

"I feel that those losses should be compensated," she told reporters at the National Press Club. She added that Turkey eagerly awaited the implementation of suspended United Nations resolution 986, which would let Iraq export limited amounts of oil through the cross-Turkey conduit in exchange for food.

Ciller, who arrived from meetings on the fringe of the U.N. General Assembly session, said Turkey had lost $27 billion since it shut the pipeline at the behest of the nascent U.S-led coalition within days of Iraq's August 2, 1990, invasion of Kuwait.

"Those in the West who are truly concerned about the future stability of Turkey should look at the damage inflicted on our economy because we stood with you for freedom and against aggression," she said in her prepared text.

Ciller said the United States had told Turkey it supported reopening the pipeline as soon as it was "physically possible," an apparent reference to the official U.S. stand on implementation of Resolution 986.

The United States says it favours letting the oil-for-food sales go ahead as soon as U.N. monitors can take up positions in Iraq to ensure that all oil revenues go into an escrow fund that pays for humanitarian aid for the Iraqi people.

U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali delayed putting the oil-for-food plan into effect after Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sent troops into a Kurdish enclave on August 31 at the request of one of two rival factions.

Under Resolution 986, the Iraqis would be allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over a 180-day period. Most of the petroleum and petroleum products would move through the pipeline, which links Iraq to the Turkish terminal of Yumurtalik.
